Title: Onyx Storm (The Empyrean, #3)
Author: Rebecca Yarros
My Review:
Definitely struggled to get through this one more than the others. The plot felt very drawn out and not important. No matter how many times Violet said “we have to go find the other dragons” or “I must find a cure NOW”, it seemed like they were just sitting around a lot and going to class.

Even towards the end of the book they were still going to class???? How is your mission to literally save the world and your boyfriend not taking front and center stage? Only once did they contemplate defying direct orders to get answers quickly, then got met with zero consequences for their actions. That should be the green light to go ahead and defy all direct orders to find a cure for Xaden and save the continent.

Speaking of Xaden, how is it that literally nothing changed from the end of book 2 to the end of book 3? The cliffhanger was nearly the same, Xaden draws upon venin powers to save someone he loves. Okay? I suppose this one has the twist of Violet losing her memory, but still? There was almost no progress for Xaden throughout this entire book.

The romance felt the same as well. Book two being “I love you but I don’t trust you” to book three being “I love you but I can’t control myself”. Toxic…

Dragons were great. Andarna leaving was tough though. Still processing how I felt about that…

Side characters were fun. However, felt very little connection to the ones that died. Felt bad for Cat though…

Overall, a decent read, but lots of filler. Wishing this had been a trilogy…

My Review:
4.5 ⭐️
This was an EXCELLENT book. Truly a great read. Brown set up an amazing dystopian society with a very interesting color system and planet system. The book starts with fantastic characters and a gut wrenching twist.

I do feel like Part 2 was quite rushed. I don’t really believe the MC as he goes through the world. That is the only reason this isn’t a 5 ⭐️.

But once we enter the academy, the story starts flying again. It was an amazing part 3 and 4. This was the closest feeling to The Hunger Games I’ve felt in a long time. Not that that is a good or bad thing, just extremely intriguing and had me at the edge of my seat till the end.

I’m very excited to see where this all goes. I completely understand needing 7 books to tell this story. The MC has a real hard time ahead of him and I can’t wait to see what happens!

Title: Katabasis
Author: R.F. Kuang
My Review:
I’ve been sitting with this one for a bit, and I keep coming back to the same feeling: ugh… at what cost?

This book has a genuinely brilliant premise. The concept is sharp, the mythological elements are compelling, and the final act — especially once Alice is on her own — is strong and emotionally satisfying. From about the 70% mark onward, the story finally delivers on the promise of its idea. I’m ultimately glad I finished it.

But it took me a month to get there.

The biggest issue for me wasn’t just pacing — it was the experience of living inside Alice’s head for nearly the entire novel. She doesn’t just endure sexism, academic abuse, and disordered eating — she internalizes and reinforces them. She repeatedly expresses beliefs like men being inherently better, feminism making women “look bad,” pride in starvation, and romanticized power imbalances with a predatory professor. And because we are almost exclusively in her POV, there’s little narrative distance or meaningful interrogation of those beliefs.

It’s one thing to portray internalized misogyny. It’s another to spend hundreds of pages immersed in it without substantial growth or reckoning.

Alice’s actions are largely driven by guilt rather than conviction — guilt over her professor, guilt over Peter — and while she does develop a backbone in the final stretch, that transformation feels abrupt because the mindset underneath it never fully evolves. The same applies to the romance: repeated betrayals are forgiven with minimal emotional repair, and reconciliation hinges more on sacrifice than earned rebuilding.

I don’t mind dark themes. I don’t mind flawed characters. But I struggled with how normalized and unchallenged the harm felt for most of the book. By the time the story truly found its momentum, I was too emotionally exhausted to rate it higher.

A fantastic premise and a strong ending — but for me, the journey to get there was frustrating enough that it ultimately lands at 2 stars.

Title: The Penelopiad
Author: Margaret Atwood
My Review:
3.5 ⭐️ Margaret Atwood’s The Penelopiad offers an intriguing reimagining of The Odyssey, retold from the perspectives of Penelope and the twelve maids. This shift in narration feels fresh, relatable, and grounded in realism.

While I appreciated the concept, I was disappointed in how Penelope’s character ultimately remained stagnant. Early on, she hints at her youthful naivety and how easily she fell for Odysseus’ tricks, suggesting potential for growth. Yet by the end, even in the afterlife, she waits passively for him as he reincarnates repeatedly, rather than moving on. Her loyalty becomes less romantic and more frustrating—especially in a story that feels like a commentary on sexual assault and the hardships faced by victims.

The dynamic between Penelope and Helen also fell short. I hoped for development that could turn their rivalry into character growth, but it stayed locked in the tired “blonde cheerleader vs. ‘ugly duckling’” trope. For a book that aimed to deconstruct the patriarchal canon, it was disappointing to see Atwood still uphold so many of its sexist tropes.

Penelope’s relationship with the maids was equally troubling. She expresses guilt over their assault and deaths, yet during the trial, she does nothing to seek justice for them. In one particularly jarring moment, she even blames them for Odysseus not staying with her:

“Why can’t you leave him alone?… Surely it’s enough! He did his penance, he said the prayers, he got himself purified!” (Pg. 190)

The trial scene itself is one of the book’s most striking and unsettling moments. The judge dismisses the maids’ case, saying:

“It would be unfortunate if this regrettable but minor incident were allowed to stand as a blot on an otherwise exceedingly distinguished career… Therefore, I must dismiss the case.” (Pg. 182)

Everyone except the maids accepts this outcome—a painfully accurate reflection of how sexual assault cases are often handled today. This realism is one of the novel’s strongest and most haunting aspects.

Perhaps the point was to show that happy endings are rare: the maids don’t get justice, Penelope never becomes truly independent, and Odysseus remains unchanged. Atwood resists the fairytale resolution, instead delivering something that mirrors the injustices and stagnation of real life. That choice, while frustrating, might be the book’s most honest message.

Title: A Touch of Chaos (Hades x Persephone Saga, #4)
Author: Scarlett St.  Clair
My Review:
1.5 ⭐️

Really thought this book would solve the problems of the last 6. With multiple POV’s I was so hopeful the story would be intriguing. We didn’t have to hear the same story told twice in two different books from both Hades and Persephone, and instead their story’s actually aligned. It started off well, but nearly DNF in the middle. Pushed through to finish and the ending was so anticlimactic.

All of these books were leading up to this Great War that was solved so quickly. Worse than that, there was no conclusion. The war ended, Hades and Persephone had sex, end of book. What happened to new Athens? What happened to Poseidon? What happened to all of Theseus followers? What happened to Zeus and Hera? What happened to Dionysus and Ari? There was ZERO conclusion.

There were so many deaths in this book. And without any mention or aftermath. So many Gods dies without characters dealing with/talking about the fallout or aftermath. What’s the point???

Also, what was with Medusa? That storyline lasted multiple books with ZERO conclusion. Where was she in the end? Like, her and Dionysus get back, and then what? Where’d she go?

And the bonus chapter at the end made no sense? After 100’s of year of Hades knowing he can’t have children, Persephone knowing he can’t have children, but still wanting to be with him, and their marriage getting approved because she can’t have children, suddenly in the last bonus chapter, they can have children?!?! With yet again, ZERO explanation???? Did the fates just revert that punishment? Nobody thought to go ask them?? We just accept have to accept it as a reader?

Also, I know there was a trigger warning, but Theseus’s chapters were ROUGH. I can usually handle a sexual assault story, but the r*pe throughout this book was extreme. Especially the last one with Ari. Chapter 37 is not for the faint of heart. TW: he r*pes Ari with her unalived sister still hanging to the end of the bed. It felt completely unnecessary.

After truly forcing myself through this series, I would not recommend it.
